summary.text: For Lemoine’s conjecture, write an odd \(k\) as \(2n+1\): for \(k>61\) the assumed representation becomes \(k=q+2p\) after swapping the two primes, while the cases \(7\le k\le61\) are covered by explicit prime decompositions. For twin primes, if all twin-prime starts were bounded, choose \(M\) above that bound, set \(K=2M+2\) and \(n=K!/2+M+1\); the auxiliary twin-prime condition forces \(p\le M\), so \(q=K!+d\) with \(d=2M+3-2p\) and \(3\le d\le K\), making \(d\) a proper divisor of the supposedly prime \(q\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let \(r_i\) denote the \(i\)-th prime when the primes are indexed starting at \(0\), so that
\[
r_0=2,\quad r_1=3,\quad r_2=5,\ldots.
\]
Thus the OEIS expression \(\operatorname{prime}(p+2)\), in which primes are indexed starting at \(1\), is \(r_{p+1}\).

Assume part (ii) of the conjecture. In this notation, the assumption is:

> For every natural number \(n>30\), there are primes \(p,q\) such that \(r_{p+1}+2\) is prime and
> \[
> 2n+1=2p+q. \tag{1}
> \]

We prove separately that this assumption implies Lemoine’s conjecture and the twin prime conjecture.

## 1. Deduction of Lemoine’s conjecture

Lemoine’s conjecture says that every odd integer \(k>5\) can be expressed as
\[
k=P+2Q
\]
with \(P,Q\) both prime.

First consider the finite range \(5<k\le 61\). Since \(k\) is odd, it is one of the odd integers from \(7\) through \(61\). Each such integer has the required representation, as displayed in the following table. In every row the two numbers on the right are prime.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
 k & \multicolumn{2}{c|}{k=P+2Q} & k & \multicolumn{2}{c}{k=P+2Q}\\ \hline
 7  &3&+2\cdot2  & 9  &3&+2\cdot3\\
 11 &5&+2\cdot3  &13  &3&+2\cdot5\\
 15 &5&+2\cdot5  &17  &3&+2\cdot7\\
 19 &5&+2\cdot7  &21  &7&+2\cdot7\\
 23 &13&+2\cdot5 &25  &3&+2\cdot11\\
 27 &5&+2\cdot11 &29  &3&+2\cdot13\\
 31 &5&+2\cdot13 &33  &7&+2\cdot13\\
 35 &13&+2\cdot11&37  &3&+2\cdot17\\
 39 &5&+2\cdot17 &41  &3&+2\cdot19\\
 43 &5&+2\cdot19 &45  &7&+2\cdot19\\
 47 &13&+2\cdot17&49  &3&+2\cdot23\\
 51 &5&+2\cdot23 &53  &7&+2\cdot23\\
 55 &17&+2\cdot19&57  &11&+2\cdot23\\
 59 &13&+2\cdot23&61  &3&+2\cdot29
\end{array}
\]

Now let \(k>61\) be odd. Write
\[
k=2n+1
\]
for a natural number \(n\). The inequality \(2n+1>61\) gives \(n>30\). Applying part (ii) to this \(n\), we obtain primes \(p,q\) satisfying (1). Therefore
\[
k=2n+1=2p+q=q+2p.
\]
Taking \(P=q\) and \(Q=p\) gives the required Lemoine representation. Notice that the additional condition that \(r_{p+1}+2\) is prime is not needed for this part of the argument. Together with the finite table, this proves Lemoine’s conjecture for every odd \(k>5\).

## 2. Deduction of the twin prime conjecture

We will prove that there are twin-prime pairs with arbitrarily large first member. This immediately implies that there are infinitely many of them: any finite set of natural numbers is bounded, whereas an arbitrarily large set is not.

We use the elementary bound
\[
r_i\ge i \qquad(i\ge0). \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, the sequence of primes is strictly increasing, and a strictly increasing sequence of natural numbers increases by at least one at each step. In fact the stronger estimate \(r_i\ge i+2\) holds, but (2) is enough. In particular,
\[
r_{p+1}\ge p+1. \tag{3}
\]

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that the first members of all twin-prime pairs are bounded. Thus there is a natural number \(a\) such that
\[
b\text{ prime and }b+2\text{ prime}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b\le a. \tag{4}
\]
Set
\[
M=\max(a,30),\qquad K=2M+2,
\]
and define
\[
n=\frac{K!}{2}+M+1. \tag{5}
\]
Since \(M\ge30\), we have \(K\ge2\), so \(2\mid K!\) and the quotient in (5) is an integer. Also \(n>M\ge30\), hence \(n>30\). We may therefore apply part (ii) to \(n\). It supplies primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
r_{p+1}+2\text{ is prime} \tag{6}
\]
and
\[
2n+1=2p+q. \tag{7}
\]
Because \(2(K!/2)=K!\), equation (5) gives
\[
2n+1=K!+2M+3.
\]
Consequently (7) becomes
\[
2p+q=K!+2M+3. \tag{8}
\]

We first show that
\[
p\le M. \tag{9}
\]
If instead \(p>M\), let \(b=r_{p+1}\). By definition, \(b\) is prime, and (6) says that \(b+2\) is prime. On the other hand, (3) and \(p>M\ge a\) yield
\[
b=r_{p+1}\ge p+1>a.
\]
This contradicts the assumed bound (4) on all twin-prime starts. Thus (9) holds.

Now define
\[
d=2M+3-2p. \tag{10}
\]
There is no issue with this subtraction in the natural numbers: by (9),
\[
2M+3-2p\ge3,
\]
so in particular
\[
d\ge3. \tag{11}
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, \(p\ge2\). Hence
\[
d=2M+3-2p\le2M+3-4=2M-1<2M+2=K. \tag{12}
\]
In particular, \(1\le d\le K\). Every positive integer at most \(K\) divides \(K!\), so
\[
d\mid K!. \tag{13}
\]

Rearranging (8) and using (10), we obtain
\[
q=K!+2M+3-2p=K!+d. \tag{14}
\]
Since \(d\mid K!\) and of course \(d\mid d\), equation (14) implies
\[
d\mid q. \tag{15}
\]
Moreover, \(K!>0\), so (14) gives
\[
d<q. \tag{16}
\]
Equations (11), (15), and (16) show that \(q\) has a divisor \(d\) satisfying
\[
1<d<q.
\]
Thus \(q\) is composite. This contradicts the fact, supplied by part (ii), that \(q\) is prime.

The contradiction proves that no bound \(a\) as in (4) exists. Therefore, for every natural number \(a\), there is some \(b>a\) for which both \(b\) and \(b+2\) are prime. Hence the set of twin-prime starts is unbounded and consequently infinite. This is precisely the twin prime conjecture.

We have proved both Lemoine’s conjecture and the twin prime conjecture from part (ii) of the A236566 conjecture.
